name: Penshurst Place
text: Your train passes the park of Penshurst Place, on the train's {side}. The house was built in 1341 for Sir John de Pulteney, four times Lord Mayor of London, and the poet Sir Philip Sidney was born there in 1554.

name: Jaques of London
text: Your train passes near Jaques of London, on the train's {side}, a games maker dating from 1795 that moved to Edenbridge in 2000. In 1849 it brought out the Staunton chess set, which became the international standard.

name: Crowhurst Yew
text: Your train passes near the Crowhurst Yew, on the train's {side}, in the churchyard at Crowhurst. It is thought to be about 4,000 years old; when a hollow was cut into it in 1820, a cannonball was found embedded in its side.

name: Brewing Industry Research Foundation
text: Your train passes near Lyttel Hall at Nutfield, on the train's {side}, bought in 1948 for the Brewing Industry Research Foundation. Its squash court became a pilot brewery, and brewing research went on there until 2024.

name: Redhill Tunnel
text: Coming into Redhill, your train passes over the covered way at the end of Redhill Tunnel. The tunnel, opened in 1899, takes the Quarry Line of the Brighton Main Line under the east of the town, so that its trains avoid Redhill station.

name: Gatton
text: Your train passes near Gatton, on the train's {side}, now just a few houses and two farms. It once sent two members to Parliament: by 1831 it had only seven voters, one of the most notorious rotten boroughs, until the Reform Act of 1832 abolished it.

name: Merstham Tunnel
text: Your train runs through Merstham Tunnel under the North Downs, opened in 1841 for the first railway from London to Brighton. Nearly 60 years later the Quarry Tunnel was built beside it, which most fast trains now use.

name: Tonbridge Priory
text: Your train passes the site of Tonbridge Priory, on the train's {side}, founded in 1124. Its last remains were demolished in 1842 when the South Eastern Railway came through, and Tonbridge's first station was built on the site.

name: Knole
text: Your train passes near Knole Park, on the train's {side}, a deer park of 1,000 acres. Its house, Knole, was once an archbishop's palace and is one of the five largest houses in England; the National Trust owns it.

name: Vine Cricket Ground
text: Your train passes near the Vine Cricket Ground in Sevenoaks, on the train's {side}, one of the oldest cricket grounds in England, first known to be used in 1734. The Duke of Dorset gave it to the town in 1773, for a rent of one peppercorn a year.

name: Polhill Anglo-Saxon cemetery
text: Your train passes near the site of the Polhill Anglo-Saxon cemetery, on the train's {side}, used in the seventh and eighth centuries. It held between 180 and 200 graves; its east end was dug in 1984, ahead of work on the M25.

name: Sevenoaks Gravel Pits
text: Your train passes near the Sevenoaks Wildlife Reserve, on the train's {side}, made from old gravel pits by the Harrison family. It was the first gravel pit in the United Kingdom turned into a nature reserve, and has five lakes filled from the River Darent.

name: Otford Roman villa
text: Your train passes near the site of a Roman villa at Otford, on the train's {side}, abandoned in the fourth century. Its remains were found and dug in the 1930s, and again in 2015.

name: Otford Palace
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Otford Palace, on the train's {side}, rebuilt by Archbishop Warham from 1514. Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon stayed there in 1520 on their way to the Field of the Cloth of Gold, and in 1537 Henry made Archbishop Cranmer hand it over to the Crown.

name: Lullingstone Roman Villa
text: Your train passes near Lullingstone Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, first built around AD 82. In the fourth century one of its rooms became a Christian chapel or house church, the earliest known in the British Isles.

name: Eynsford Castle
text: Your train passes near Eynsford Castle, on the train's {side}, a ruin now looked after by English Heritage. William de Eynsford built it, probably between 1085 and 1087, to protect the lands of the Archbishop of Canterbury.

name: St John's Jerusalem
text: Your train passes near St John's Jerusalem, on the train's {side}, set up in 1199 by the Knights Hospitaller. Its 13th-century chapel and a garden moated by the River Darent belong to the National Trust and are open to the public.

name: South Darenth viaduct
text: Your train crosses the viaduct at South Darenth, built in 1859 and 1860 to a design by Joseph Cubitt. It has ten arches, each about 20 metres high, and one of them spans the River Darent.

name: White Horse Stone
text: Your train passes near the White Horse Stone, on the train's {side}, a sarsen stone on Blue Bell Hill. Excavators found a Neolithic longhouse just south of it, 18 metres long, in use some time between about 4100 and 3500 BC.

name: Medway Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the River Medway on the viaduct of the high-speed line to the Channel Tunnel, finished in 2002 beside the two bridges of the M2. In 2003 a specially formed Eurostar crossed it at 208 mph, a new speed record for Britain's railways.

name: Baker's Hole
text: Your train passes near Baker's Hole, on the train's {side}, a filled-in quarry by Ebbsfleet. Quarrymen there found many Stone Age flint tools from 1909, and it has been called the best known site in Britain from its part of the Old Stone Age.

name: St George's Church, Gravesend
text: Your train passes near St George's Church in Gravesend, on the train's {side}, where Pocahontas was buried in 1617. She died in Gravesend aged 20 or 21, on her way home to America; a bronze statue of her stands by the church.

name: Stonebridge Road
text: Your train passes near Stonebridge Road, on the train's {side}, the football ground built in 1905 for Northfleet United. It is the home of Ebbsfleet United, and holds 4,769 people.

name: Swanscombe Skull Site
text: Your train passes near the Swanscombe Skull Site, on the train's {side}, an old gravel pit. In 1935 and 1936 an amateur found pieces of a human skull there, about 400,000 years old, probably from an early Neanderthal or Homo heidelbergensis.

name: Ingress Abbey
text: Your train passes near Ingress Abbey, on the train's {side}, a mansion built by the Thames in 1833 for the solicitor James Harmer. Harmer served as a model for Jaggers, the lawyer in Dickens's Great Expectations.

name: Holy Trinity Church, Dartford
text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church in Dartford, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1080 by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester. A painting of St George slaying the dragon, from about 1485, can still be seen on one of its walls.

name: Dartford Priory
text: Your train passes near what is left of Dartford Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Dominican nuns founded by Edward III. Henry VIII took it for himself and turned it into a royal manor house; its gatehouse survives in a farmhouse.

name: Guru Nanak Darbar Gurdwara
text: Your train passes the Guru Nanak Darbar Gurdwara in Gravesend, on the train's {side}, one of the largest Sikh gurdwaras outside India. It opened in 2010, at a cost of £12 million.

name: Higham and Strood tunnel
text: Your train runs through the Higham and Strood tunnel, 3.5 km long, dug by hand for the Thames and Medway Canal. From 1845 trains shared it with the barges, on a single track resting partly on the towpath. In 1846 the railway bought the tunnel, filled in the canal and laid two tracks.

name: Temple Manor
text: Your train passes Temple Manor in Strood, on the train's {side}, built in the early 13th century for the Knights Templar. When the Templars were suppressed in 1312 it passed to the Knights Hospitaller; English Heritage now opens it to visitors.

name: Ranscombe Farm
text: Your train passes near Ranscombe Farm, on the train's {side}, a working farm and Plantlife nature reserve. It is known for rare plants of farmland and chalk grassland, such as hairy mallow, ground pine and the lady orchid.

name: Holborough Marshes
text: Your train passes Holborough Marshes, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of 35 hectares on the edge of Snodland, run by Kent Wildlife Trust. It has reedbeds and wet grassland, with water voles, reed buntings and sedge warblers.

name: All Saints Church, Snodland
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Snodland, on the train's {side}, which stands where the Pilgrims' Way crosses the River Medway. It is mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086, and the church standing today was begun in the 12th century.

name: Aylesford Priory
text: Your train passes near Aylesford Priory, The Friars, on the train's {side}, founded in 1242 by Carmelite friars who came from Mount Carmel in the Holy Land. The Carmelites came back in 1949, and it is a place of pilgrimage once more.

name: Allington Castle
text: Your train passes near Allington Castle, on the train's {side}, home of Sir Thomas Wyatt the Younger until the Crown seized it in 1554, after his rebellion against Queen Mary. Largely a ruin by the early 1900s, it was saved and restored by Sir Martin Conway and his wife.

name: Archbishop's Palace, Maidstone
text: Your train passes near the Archbishop's Palace in Maidstone, on the train's {side}, by the River Medway. It was a resting place for archbishops travelling between London and Canterbury, and work on the present building began in 1348.

name: East Farleigh Bridge
text: Your train passes East Farleigh Bridge, on the train's {side}, probably built in the 14th century and still carrying traffic, one way at a time, over the Medway. It has been described as probably the finest medieval bridge in the south of England.

name: Teston Bridge
text: Your train passes Teston Bridge, on the train's {side}, a narrow bridge over the Medway built in the 14th or 15th century. The line crosses its road on the level, where Teston Crossing Halt stood from 1909 to 1959.

name: Nettlestead Place
text: Your train passes Nettlestead Place, on the train's {side}, a ragstone house begun around 1250. It was used as an oast house for two centuries before it was restored as a home in the 1920s.

name: The Hop Farm
text: Your train passes near the Hop Farm at Beltring, on the train's {side}, where hops have been grown since at least the 16th century. It has the largest collection of oast houses in the world, and once grew hops for Whitbread.
